A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VCTK bandwidth-extension work, renamed from NDSI-BWE to CIS-BWE. All pages, figures, tables and v2 Appendices A.1–A.9 were inspected. V1's blank table cells and placeholder figures are visible document features, not extraction failures.

before.justification: V1 reports original discriminator and generator ablations, bandwidth-extension scores and computational measurements in Tables 1–5. Its claimed listening study lacks reported outcomes, but the objective experiments establish original empirical results.

after.justification: V2 retains original objective experiments, expands baseline results and reports MOS and preference outcomes in Figure 4, with listening-study details in Appendix A.9.

M1.justification: The dual-stream Lattice/ConformerNeXt generator and final four-discriminator combination are retained. V2 newly specifies losses and per-scale SRDs without establishing whether these changed the procedure or document existing implementation. Its MRLD description also says 2D convolution while Figure 2 and Table 7 specify 1D, preventing a reliable judgment about an actual architectural change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate English VCTK speech across the same nine bandwidth-extension ranges. V2's listening study uses ranges already covered in v1. TTS/ASR applications and noisy/reverberant robustness are discussed without documenting additional evaluated tasks or environments.

E2.justification: V2 Table 4 establishes measured comparisons with EBEN and AERO, whose v1 Table 3 rows contain no performance scores. AP-BWE remains, while MS-BWE and its two reported LSD entries are removed. NU-Wave's empty row also disappears, but v1 provides no results establishing its evaluated participation.

E3.justification: The reported listening panel changes from five judges in v1's abstract to ten in v2 Section 3.11 and Appendix A.9. The stated 50-epoch budget, batch size, optimizer settings and six objective metrics remain unchanged. Newly disclosed splits, segmentation and listening procedures do not establish changes to previously used procedures.

E4.justification: The discriminator, generator and frequency-range analyses are largely retained, with one revised generator-ablation result. V2 adds a male/female MOS breakdown and a concrete reconstruction example replacing dummy spectrograms. The subgroup definition is inconsistent: Section 3.11 refers to speakers, whereas Appendix A.9 refers to participants.

E5.justification: Appendix A.3 and Table 9 newly disclose seed 1234. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's claims of significant listener preference are not accompanied by a statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds complete EBEN/AERO scores and listening outcomes: Figure 4 reports overall MOS 4.42 versus AP-BWE's 4.36 and preferences of 52% versus 41%. The proposed model's reported LSD values change from 0.98/0.79/0.79 to 0.95/0.72/0.71 across the three main ranges; PESQ changes at two ranges. The linear-generator ablation's NISQA-MOS changes from 4.32 to 3.72. Frequency-range and computational tables otherwise retain their values.

T1.justification: V2 Section 2.3 and Table 1 add explicit mathematical definitions of the weighted generator losses and summed discriminator hinge objective, including Equations 4–5. The Lyapunov estimator, reconstruction equations and convolution-complexity reasoning are retained. No theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central chaos-informed discriminator and Lattice/ConformerNeXt contributions remain. V2 narrows the abstract's four-new/seven-total discriminator account to the two proposed chaos-informed critics, aligning it with the existing method. It drops v1's faster-inference promise and shifts application emphasis toward TTS and ASR; the 40x discriminator-size and approximately half-parameter claims already appeared in v1's body.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 expands the mechanism explanation through vocal-fold/vocal-tract coupling and intermittent chaos. V2 removes explicit limitations concerning low-resource generalization and extra training/inference time while retaining the single-dataset, noise-free restriction. Appendix A.9 nevertheless newly interprets listening results as noisy/reverberant robustness without documenting such testing, and its 2% preference advantage conflicts with Figure 4's 11-point margin.

D1.justification: V2 adds loss weights, the 102/8-speaker split, 8,000-sample crops, STFT settings, layerwise parameter breakdowns, inference instructions, listening procedures and approximately 25-minute epochs. It identifies the AP-BWE codebase as its implementation basis and promises code after acceptance. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although Table 9's one-GPU setting conflicts with Section 3.2's four GPUs, and some discriminator specifications remain inconsistent.

R1.justification: The integrated introduction and related work substantially expand coverage of modern BWE, phase modeling, discriminator families, TTS/ASR applications and physiological chaos. Appendix A.1 adds extensive research context for speech dynamics. New references include Peng et al., Kong et al., Herzel et al., Feng et al. and Haws and Cui; v2 also explicitly acknowledges its substantial adaptation of AP-BWE code.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion, merges introduction and related work, renames the model throughout and replaces the original repetitive opening with a structured motivation and contribution list. It also adds dedicated loss and subjective-analysis sections, acknowledgments and a nine-part appendix.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the mismatched architecture drawing and duplicated dummy spectrograms with a relevant architecture diagram, discriminator schematic and reconstruction example. It adds MOS/preference plots, the listening interface, a loss table and three implementation tables. The baseline table also changes metric order and row formatting, beyond its numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V1 lacks an explicit training objective, contains a mismatched architecture figure and leaves most baseline comparisons unreported. V2 substantially resolves these deficiencies through loss definitions, relevant diagrams, detailed implementation documentation, completed EBEN/AERO comparisons and actual listening outcomes. Removing MS-BWE and introducing conflicting hardware, discriminator and subjective-result descriptions limit confidence; unsupported robustness language also weakens interpretation. Nevertheless, the gains in completeness and assessability clearly outweigh these problems relative to the visibly unfinished v1.
